summary: Trend Detective helps students and the public act as data detectives with NASA Earth data. Users pick one of 40 variables, each with a plain definition, from temperature and rain to evaporation, runoff, groundwater, NO2, CO2 and methane (MERRA-2, GPM, GLDAS, AIRS, OMI, OCO-2, MODIS, POWER). They draw a rectangle on a 3D globe and choose the dates. The app fetches the data from NASA, removes the seasonal cycle and builds the region’s monthly time series. It reports the rate of change per decade with a 95% confidence interval, and tests significance with an autocorrelation-corrected t-test and the Mann-Kendall test. A plain-language verdict explains the result, and an optional AI assistant answers follow-up questions and flags any number not in the results. Because one cause can push a variable up in one place and down in another, a heatmap on the globe shows, for map variables, where inside the region the trend is significant, corrected for testing many cells at once. When a trend isn’t significant yet, the app estimates how many more years of data it needs.
details:
Trend Detective answers one question about NASA Earth data: is this really changing here, or could it be chance?

  1. Pick a variable. A browser like Giovanni's lists 40 variables by topic (air, air quality, water, land and plants, ocean, snow and ice), with search and a plain-language definition for each. They come from MERRA-2, GLDAS, GPM IMERG, AIRS, OMI, OCO-2, NOBM, MODIS and NASA POWER. Users can also upload their own CSV.
  2. Pick a place and years. Draw a rectangle on a 3D globe, or type its edges, and choose the dates. Choose what to make: the trend tests, a trend map, a month-by-month map, or any mix.
  3. Fetch. The backend gets the data live from NASA Harmony, Giovanni, POWER and AppEEARS with an Earthdata token, shows NASA's own progress, and caches every result so a rerun takes seconds.
  4. Prepare. It cleans the values, converts units and takes each month's difference from its own normal, so the seasons don't pass for a trend. It then averages the rectangle with latitude weights and records how much of the area had data each month.
  5. Test. Least squares with a t-test corrected for autocorrelation, its 95% confidence interval, and Mann-Kendall with Sen's slope alongside. Further checks: a block shuffle test, the Pettitt test for a sudden shift, residual checks, outlier months, the trend over every stretch of years, the trend for each month of the year, and how many years of data it would take to detect a trend this size.
  6. Explain. The verdict reads "Rising, and unlikely to be chance", "Falling…" or "No clear trend yet", with the rate per decade and its likely range. "Why we think so" draws the evidence as charts, and the caveats sit next to the result.
  7. Map it. For map variables, every grid cell gets its own test, with a false discovery rate correction across cells. The heatmap on the globe outlines the cells that pass, and clicking a cell opens its chart. A slider plays the months back on the globe.
  8. Ask. "In plain words" writes an overview from the numbers without any AI model. With their own AI key (Anthropic or OpenAI-compatible), or a local model such as Ollama, users can ask follow-up questions, and the app flags any number in an answer that isn't in the results.

Benefits

  • Students learn the method, not only the answer. They see why a trend can be real, chance, too short to call, or "not yet": a trend may need more years to become significant, and the app says how many.
  • It is honest by design. A record under 10 years is never called a trend, disagreement between tests is reported, and so are sudden shifts and outlier months.
  • It is checked against a published result: on NOAA's Mauna Loa CO2 record, our trend comes within 0.02 ppm a year of the growth NOAA reports.
  • It is free and open source. It runs locally with Docker and a free Earthdata account, and the AI part works without any paid key.

Intended impact

We want high-school and college students, and the science-literate public, to become data detectives. They should be able to test a trend claim from the news against NASA data themselves, and to understand that one process can push a variable up in one place and down in another. Eight one-click examples teach the method: Europe warming, CO2 and methane rising, cleaner air over China, groundwater falling in northwest India, farmland greening in Punjab, India warming in some places and cooling in others, and London rain with no clear trend.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

  • Languages: Go 1.27 (gateway, ingest, narrator), Python 3.14 (preprocess, analysis) and TypeScript (web).
  • Science: numpy, scipy, xarray and netCDF4.
  • Web: React 19, Vite 8 and Bun, MapLibre GL 6 in globe projection with OpenFreeMap / OpenStreetMap styles, and d3 for SVG charts.
  • Services: NATS JetStream for the job queue, Redis for job state, SeaweedFS as S3 storage, nginx, and Docker Compose.
  • Contracts: Protocol Buffers with buf, and Connect between the browser and the gateway.
  • Monitoring: OpenTelemetry, Jaeger, Prometheus, Pyroscope and Grafana.
  • Testing: GitHub Actions CI for each service.
  • NASA services: Harmony, Giovanni, CMR, AppEEARS, POWER and Earthdata Login.
  • Hardware: no special hardware, only our own laptops.

How it is creative

  • Trend maps on a 3D globe. Each cell is coloured by its own trend and outlined only if it survives the multiple-testing correction, so the map doesn't light up by chance.
  • The p-value made visible. The shuffle test is drawn as a histogram of fake trends, with the real one marked.
  • The trend triangle. It shows whether a result depends on the years picked.
  • "Not yet significant". The app shows how many years of data a trend would need.
  • An AI narrator that is checked. It explains only computed numbers, and any number in its answer that isn't in the results is flagged.
  • Month-by-month playback of the grid, so users can watch a trend build or a heatwave pass.

Factors we considered

  • Audience: every number comes with a sentence, and every variable with a definition.
  • Statistical pitfalls:
    • seasonal cycles, handled with anomalies whose normals are fitted with a trend;
    • autocorrelation, handled with an effective sample size and the Hamed-Rao correction;
    • gaps and partial coverage;
    • short records;
    • sudden shifts and outliers;
    • testing many map cells at once.
  • Data access: Earthdata Login and NASA's download chain don't suit a browser, so all data calls run on a backend. Preflight checks, caching and a task cap protect NASA quotas.
  • Data choices:
    • monthly products, since hourly data is far larger;
    • no joining of different data versions;
    • AIRS and MERRA-2 alongside MODIS, whose science data ends in 2027.
  • Privacy: a user's AI key stays in page memory and is never stored or logged

All data is accessed through NASA Harmony (subsetting and Giovanni area averages), the Giovanni time-series API, CMR, AppEEARS and the POWER API, with Earthdata Login
dataRefs: NASA POWER: air temperature and rain at a point
GLDAS Noah monthly: soil moisture at the top and in the root zone, soil temperature, evaporation, runoff, snow water and snow depth; and GLDAS CLSM groundwater
AIRS on Aqua, monthly level 3 (AIRS3STM v7): water vapour, air and surface temperature, cloud cover, ozone, and methane as a column average
projectRefs: MODIS MOD13A3 NDVI and MOD11A2 land surface temperature, through AppEEARS (LP DAAC).
